channel.title: Usukh-Erdene Choijamts — Writing
channel.description: Notes on things I've built and broken. Writing about your work is the cheapest way to show how you think — recruiters read these.

item.title: How this portfolio stays fast without a framework
item.description: A static site generator in 400 lines of Node, no dependencies, and what that buys you on the Lighthouse report.
item.content:encoded:
Most portfolio sites ship a JavaScript framework to render text that never changes. That felt like the wrong trade for a page whose entire job is to load instantly and say who I am, so this one is generated at build time and served as plain HTML.

The whole build

There are three moving parts:

  1. content.js — every piece of copy on the site, in one object
  2. posts/*.md — writing, as markdown with frontmatter
  3. build.js — reads both, writes static HTML

No bundler, no framework, and no node_modules. npm install does nothing because there is nothing to install. CI goes from checkout to deployed in about twenty seconds.

What that buys you

The numbers that actually move a Lighthouse score:

DecisionEffect
CSS inlined into <head>No render-blocking stylesheet request
System font stackNo font download, no layout shift on swap
defer on the only scriptParsing never blocks on JavaScript
Static HTMLLargest Contentful Paint is the first response

The last one is the one people underrate. If your hero text is rendered by JavaScript, your LCP cannot happen until the bundle downloads, parses, and executes. If it is in the HTML, LCP is bounded by your network round trip and nothing else.

Progressive enhancement, not decoration

Every interactive piece degrades cleanly:

  • The theme toggle reads localStorage in a tiny inline script before first paint, so there is no flash of the wrong colours. If storage is blocked, it falls back to the OS preference.
  • The rotating hero text is server-rendered with its first word already in place. JavaScript only animates it, and skips entirely under prefers-reduced-motion.
  • The scroll reveal only hides elements once JavaScript has confirmed it is running. Without it, nothing is hidden.
  • The contact form is a real <form> with a real action. fetch makes it feel nicer; turning JavaScript off just makes it submit normally.

The test I use: disable JavaScript, reload, and check that the page is still complete and readable. If something disappears, it was decoration pretending to be structure.

The one piece of cleverness

The social preview image is generated by writing PNG chunks directly with Node's zlib:

return Buffer.concat([
  Buffer.from([0x89, 0x50, 0x4e, 0x47, 0x0d, 0x0a, 0x1a, 0x0a]),
  chunk("IHDR", ihdr),
  chunk("IDAT", zlib.deflateSync(raw, { level: 9 })),
  chunk("IEND", Buffer.alloc(0)),
]);

It renders the name in a 5x7 bitmap font over a gradient. That is absurd for one image — until you price the alternative, which is adding Puppeteer to a project that otherwise has no dependencies at all.

The point is not that frameworks are bad. It is that this particular page has no state, no interactivity worth the name, and one job: be fast and say something true. Matching the tool to that job took less code than configuring a build system would have.

item.title: TODO: What I learned building [project]
item.description: TODO: One sentence that makes someone want to read this. Be specific about the problem, not the technology.
item.content:encoded:
This is a template. Replace it or delete the file.

The most valuable thing you can put in a portfolio is evidence of how you think. A post that walks through one real decision does more than a list of frameworks ever will. Here is a structure that works.

The problem

Open with the concrete situation. What was broken, slow, or missing? Give a number if you have one — "the dashboard took 6 seconds to load" beats "the dashboard was slow", because the number proves you measured.

What I tried first

Say what did not work. This is the part almost everyone skips, and it is the part that reads as genuine experience. An engineer who only ever describes their successful approach sounds like they are describing someone else's.

What actually worked

Explain the fix and, more importantly, why it worked:

  • What was the actual root cause?
  • What made this solution the right shape for it?
  • What did you deliberately choose not to do, and why?

Show the code if a snippet makes it land:

// A short, real snippet beats a long, invented one.
// Ten lines is usually plenty.

What it cost

Every decision has a downside. Naming yours is the strongest possible signal that you understand the tradeoff rather than having copied it from a blog post. Was it more complexity? Extra memory? A dependency you now maintain?

What I would do differently

Close with the honest retrospective. This is what an interviewer will actually ask you about, so having thought it through in writing means you will answer it well out loud.

Writing tips for this section of your portfolio:

  • Three good posts beat ten thin ones. Do not pad the list.
  • Write about work you can discuss in depth — you will be asked.
  • Date them honestly. A gap is fine; a fake date is not.
  • Delete this template once you have written a real post.
